summary:
Kalmykia, an autonomous republic within Russia, stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when President Vladimir Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage is prohibited and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

The expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Penalties reach fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences risk criminal prosecution. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Human Rights Watch documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, alongside the 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 compared with 22 in 2021-22. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

Raid practice is documented. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that "Ada", a transgender woman, was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. That note, the framework under which Kalmykia is assessed, contains no Kalmykia-specific information beyond the national picture.
tangentialFactors:
Sub-national variation inside Russia has been documented for one region only. The UK Home Office note names Chechnya alongside the country as a whole when identifying LGBT+ people as a particular social group, and no comparable reporting exists for Kalmykia; a visitor's exposure here follows the national statutes rather than any identifiable local enforcement pattern.

Temper of the crackdown: the Supreme Court designation produced raids within 48 hours, an extremism conviction count of 101 within eighteen months, and an administrative-symbol docket of 98 cases since January 2024. The scale of penalties escalated alongside the breadth of conduct covered, moving from fines for speech to prison terms of up to 12 years for alleged affiliation.

Detention carries documented lethal risk. The death of a man held on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency, reported in December 2024, and the forced confinement of a transgender woman in a conversion-therapy facility for nine months indicate harms that follow from enforcement rather than from the sentence itself.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot obtain legal gender recognition. The 2023 statute bars gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year, so medical transition and documentary change are both unavailable domestically.

Residents live without statutory protection: the constitution provides no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people, and consensual same-sex activity, though not criminalised, offers no basis for marriage or partner recognition.

Ordinary online expression is a residency risk. Of the 81 people found guilty under article 20.3 since January 2024, the displays were made mostly on social media, and the 257 propaganda penalties of 2023-24 were imposed on residents as well as on organisations and media.

The UK Home Office note records no division-specific findings for Kalmykia, so residents here are assessed under the same national standard applied countrywide, including the particular-social-group recognition used for refugee convention claims.
